section.title: Robbing God in Tithes
section.sectionRationale: The fifth disputation rests on God's unchanging faithfulness: because I the LORD do not change, you are not destroyed. On that ground God calls the people to return, and when they ask how, He names their withholding of tithes and offerings as robbery of God, inviting them to test Him with wholehearted giving and see His blessing poured out.
section.thesis: Because God does not change, He keeps calling His faithless people to return; their withheld tithes reveal hearts that rob God, but He invites them to test His faithfulness with obedient giving and promises blessing beyond measure.
section.frameNote: Two beats: the unchanging God who calls His people to return, and the charge of robbing God in tithes and offerings, with the striking invitation to test God and watch the windows of heaven open.

units.label: I the LORD do not change
units.note: return to Me, and I will return to you

verses.text: “Because I, the LORD, do not {{shanah|change}}, you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed.

Yet from the days of your fathers, you have turned away from My statutes and have not kept them. {{shuv|Return}} to Me, and I will return to you,” says the LORD of Hosts. “But you ask, ‘How can we return?’

units.label: Will a man rob God
units.note: test Me, and see the windows of heaven open

verses.text: Will a man {{qaba|rob}} God? Yet you are robbing Me! But you ask, ‘How do we rob You?’ In {{maaser|tithes}} and offerings.
You are cursed with a curse, yet you, the whole nation, are still robbing Me.

Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house. {{bachan|Test}} Me in this,” says the LORD of Hosts. “See if I will not open the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing without measure.
I will rebuke the devourer for you, so that it will not destroy the fruits of your land, and the vine in your field will not fail to produce fruit,” says the LORD of Hosts.
“Then all the nations will call you blessed, for you will be a land of delight,” says the LORD of Hosts.

shanah.gloss: To change, to alter, to become different. God declares I do not change, pointing to His constancy in character and covenant. This unchanging faithfulness is the reason a faithless people has not been consumed, and it is the ground on which He keeps calling them to return.

shuv.gloss: To turn, return, repent. The great prophetic word for repentance: return to Me, and I will return to you. It describes a turning of the whole life back to God, and the mutual movement pictures a God who draws near to those who draw near to Him.

qaba.gloss: To rob, defraud, take by force what belongs to another. God charges that in withholding tithes the people were actually robbing Him. The word is startling: it reframes stinginess toward God not as a minor lapse but as theft from the One who owns all.

maaser.gloss: A tenth, a tithe. Under the law the tithe supported the priests, the temple, and the poor. Here the people's failure to bring the full tithe left God's house without provision and exposed hearts that trusted their possessions more than the God who gave them.

bachan.gloss: To test, prove, examine, as metal is assayed. God rarely invites testing, yet here He does: test Me in this. It is not a licence for greedy bargaining but an invitation to prove His faithfulness by wholehearted obedience and watch Him provide.

basic.context: God grounds His appeal in His own unchanging character: because I do not change, you have not been destroyed. He calls the people to return, and when they ask how, He points to their tithes. They had been withholding what belonged to God, and He calls it robbery. Then He gives a remarkable challenge: bring the full tithe and test Me, and see whether I do not pour out blessing.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage is often misused as a formula for guaranteed wealth. Read rightly, it addresses a specific covenant people under the law of the tithe, and its heart is trust: will they trust God enough to give obediently? The New Testament calls for generous, cheerful, sacrificial giving rather than a fixed percentage, but the principle stands that we cannot out-give God.
basic.originalLanguages: God declares He does not shanah, change, which is why He keeps calling His people to shuv, return. They had been withholding the maaser, the tithe, which God calls qaba, robbing Him. Then He invites them to bachan, to test Him, by bringing the full tithe and watching heaven open.
basic.typology: God's unchanging faithfulness that spares an undeserving people points to the steadfast grace fulfilled in Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever. The storehouse filled so there is food in God's house anticipates the abundance of the gospel, where God supplies every need in Christ.
basic.christ: The unchanging God of verse 6 is revealed in Jesus Christ, who is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Hebrews 13:8. The one who would not let His people be destroyed is the God who so loved the world that He gave His Son, the ultimate proof that we cannot out-give God. Christ, who was rich yet became poor for us, teaches us to give freely as we have freely received.
basic.god: God is unchanging, and that constancy is pure mercy: it is why sinners are not consumed. He is faithful, calling His wayward people home again and again. He is generous, ready to pour out blessing without measure. And He is worthy of our trust, inviting His people to prove His faithfulness by obedient giving.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 13:8 says Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, the unchanging God of verse 6. Second Corinthians 9 teaches cheerful, generous giving and God's abundant supply. Luke 6:38 promises that the measure we give will be given back, pressed down and overflowing.
basic.oneStory: God's unchanging faithfulness is the thread that holds the whole Bible together and keeps a rebellious people from destruction. That constancy runs straight to Christ, the same forever, in whom God pours out blessing without measure on all who return to Him.

context.literary:
The unit is a frame around a single exchange. Verses 6 and 7 are the opening, with a statement of God's constancy and a call to return. Verses 8 to 12 are the argument, shaped like a court case. The accusation comes first, 'Will a man rob God?', then the protest, then the evidence, 'In tithes and offerings,' then the verdict, 'You are cursed with a curse,' and finally the offer, 'Bring the full tithe.' Unlike the threats that close several of the earlier disputations, this one ends with an invitation.

Two word pairs run through it. The first is return. The call in verse 7, 'Return to Me, and I will return to you,' is two verbs from the same root, one for the people and one for God, so that the offer is reciprocal and nothing is asked of them that He does not first promise. The second pair is curse and blessing, which move in opposite directions across the passage. Verse 9 begins in curse, verse 10 offers blessing without measure, and verse 12 ends with all the nations calling the people blessed. The movement is from curse to blessing, and the hinge is the obedience of verse 10.

A second movement is from the nation to the nations. In verse 9 the whole nation, the one goy, is robbing God. In verse 12 all the nations, the plural goyim, will call them blessed. The same Hebrew word appears in the singular and the plural, and the prophet turns a nation's failure into a nation's witness. Alongside this is a movement from the temple to the world: the 'storehouse' of verse 10 is the place where God's food supply is kept, and the effect of filling it is felt in fields and vineyards in verse 11.

In the book as a whole, this disputation follows the complaint about justice and precedes the complaint that serving God is futile, 3:13 to 15. It stands as the practical test of whether the returning of verse 7 is real or only talk.
context.historical:
The tithe was not an abstract rule but the working budget of the temple. Numbers 18:21 assigns the tithes of Israel to the Levites in return for their service at the Tent of Meeting, and Numbers 18:26 asks the Levites to give a tenth of what they receive to the priests, a 'tithe of the tithe.' Deuteronomy 14:28 to 29 adds a tithe every third year to be laid up within the towns for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. Tithes were paid in produce, grain, wine and oil, since Judah's wealth was in the land. When the people stopped bringing them, the temple staff were the ones who went hungry.

Nehemiah shows exactly what happened. In his pledge the community promised to bring the firstfruits and the tithe to the storerooms of the house of God, Nehemiah 10:37 to 38. Later he found that 'the portions for the Levites had not been given to them,' so that the Levites and singers 'had gone back to their own fields,' Nehemiah 13:10. He asked the officials, 'Why has the house of God been neglected?' and restored the tithes to the storerooms, 13:11 to 12. Malachi is speaking into the same neglect.

The economic pressure was real and not an excuse invented by the greedy. Haggai describes a people who 'planted much but harvested little,' Haggai 1:6, with blight, mildew and hail, Haggai 2:17. Nehemiah records those who had to mortgage their fields and borrow money to pay the king's tax, Nehemiah 5:3 to 4. A farmer facing a poor year would find the tenth for God the easiest to hold back. Malachi's answer is that holding it back is itself part of the cycle of loss, since the curse of verse 9 is the poor harvest the people are trying to protect themselves from.

The Persian authorities' own taxes competed with the temple's claim. In this setting the tithe was a statement of whose land it really was. It declared that the land was God's gift and that the first claim on its produce was His.
context.canonical:
The practice of giving a tenth is older than Moses. Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything, Genesis 14:20, and Jacob vowed at Bethel, 'of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth,' Genesis 28:22. That second text matters for the opening of Malachi's unit, since God addresses the people as 'descendants of Jacob' in verse 6, and they are failing to do what their ancestor promised. The law then fixed the practice in Leviticus 27, Numbers 18 and Deuteronomy 14 and 26.

The blessing of verses 10 to 12 draws on the covenant blessings of Deuteronomy 28. 'The windows of heaven' echo the heavens opened as God's abundant storehouse, Deuteronomy 28:12, and the 'devourer' of verse 11 answers the locusts that consume the seed of the disobedient, Deuteronomy 28:38. The curse of verse 9 is the curse of Deuteronomy 28:15 to 18. Proverbs gives the same truth in wisdom form: 'Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your harvest; then your barns will be filled with plenty,' Proverbs 3:9 to 10. Haggai's 'from this day on, I will bless you,' Haggai 2:19, is the immediate historical parallel.

The New Testament does not repeat the command but keeps the principle and enlarges it. Jesus affirms tithing while rebuking those who neglect 'justice, mercy, and faithfulness,' Matthew 23:23 and Luke 11:42. Hebrews 7:1 to 5 notes that Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek, a greater priest. Paul treats giving as a grace, 2 Corinthians 8:1 to 5 and 9:6 to 8, a regular habit, 1 Corinthians 16:2, and supports those who minister, 1 Corinthians 9:13 to 14. The widow with her two copper coins in Mark 12:41 to 44 shows that the measure has moved from a percentage to the whole heart.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Malachi intends to show his hearers that their relationship with God has a practical shape, and that a gap between what they say and what they bring is a revealing one. They protest that they have not turned away. The prophet answers by pointing to something checkable, the contents of the storerooms. He does not accuse them of abstract disloyalty but of a concrete withholding which any of them could confirm in a moment.

He also means to correct their reading of their hardships. The people believed they were poor because the times were hard and so could not afford the tithe. Malachi turns the cause around: the times are hard because the tithe is withheld, and the way out of the loss is to trust God with the first portion. This is a hard word to a struggling community, and he knows it, which is why he gives the challenge in the form of an invitation, 'Test Me in this.'

Behind both aims is the aim of the whole disputation, that the people might see God as He is. The opening line of the unit says that He does not change. The tithe is the place where they can prove it. The prophet wants the community to discover, by obeying, that the God who commands the tenth is the God who 'opens the windows of heaven,' and that their fear of scarcity was unfounded. At the end, he wants Judah to become what Abraham was promised, a people through whom the nations see God's goodness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The command to bring the full tithe was given to a particular people under a particular covenant. The tithe funded the Levites, who had no land, and supported the poor in the third year. Its blessings were the covenant blessings of Deuteronomy 28, rain, harvest and protection from pests, promised to a nation living in a land. Reading verse 10 as a law of the church that guarantees a financial return to anyone who gives ten percent is therefore to move the verse out of its setting twice, once from the covenant and once from the land.

What carries over is wider than the percentage. The principle that God has first claim on what we have, that withholding from Him is a form of distrust, and that He is generous beyond measure, runs through the New Testament. Paul does not cite Malachi; he teaches that giving should be generous, voluntary and cheerful, 2 Corinthians 9:6 to 8, regular and proportionate, 1 Corinthians 16:2, and that those who teach are to be supported, 1 Corinthians 9:13 to 14. Many Christians treat the tithe as a floor and a useful discipline, while others hold that the New Testament standard is higher than ten percent for some and different for others. Either way, the New Testament takes away the transaction and leaves the trust.

The promise of blessing is likewise not a formula. The New Testament says God will supply the needs of those who give, 2 Corinthians 9:8, but the 'blessing' of the new covenant is first of all 'every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms,' Ephesians 1:3, and Paul holds up as his example a poor church that gave beyond its means in the midst of ordeal, 2 Corinthians 8:2. The Macedonians are the answer to anyone who reads Malachi as a promise of wealth.

debates.question: Is Malachi 3:10 an invitation to test God, and how does that fit with 'Do not test the LORD your God'?

views.label: God invites a test that He has the right to set
views.case: Deuteronomy 6:16 forbids testing the LORD 'as you tested Him at Massah,' where the people demanded water in unbelief. In Malachi, God Himself sets the terms and invites the trial, and the test is of obedience and trust, not of His patience. Isaiah 7:11 to 12 shows the other side: Ahaz refuses a sign God offered and is rebuked for it. Psalm 34:8 invites the same experiment, 'Taste and see that the LORD is good.' The line is drawn between a test demanded in doubt and a test offered by God.

views.label: A covenant promise, specific to Israel
views.case: Others stress that the offer is to a covenant nation under Deuteronomy 28, so that it cannot be lifted over into a general promise. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:16 to the devil, Matthew 4:7, and refuses to force God's hand. On this view, the Malachi invitation holds only as part of the old covenant arrangement and is fulfilled in the gift of the Spirit and the supply of need in Christ.

views.label: A promise that gives a general principle of trust
views.case: A third group holds that the specific blessings were covenantal but the principle is permanent, that God honors those who put Him first. Proverbs 3:9 to 10 and Luke 6:38 express it, while Paul's teaching in 2 Corinthians 9 gives it a New Testament form. They stress that the reward is not guaranteed to be material.

debates.bearing: Under every reading, the invitation is to trust God with something that costs us, not to use Him as a lever. The test does not fail if the harvest does not improve, since the passage's real claim is about the character of the One who is trusted. A reader who gives in order to get has missed what the passage is for.

debates.question: Is the tithe binding on Christians today?

views.label: No, it belonged to the Mosaic law
views.case: The tithe was part of the system that supported the Levites and the temple. The New Testament nowhere commands Gentile believers to tithe, and the Jerusalem council did not impose it, Acts 15:28 to 29. Paul speaks of generosity and cheerfulness, not a fixed fraction, 2 Corinthians 9:7. Hebrews says the priesthood that received the tithe has been replaced, Hebrews 7:12.

views.label: Yes, as a continuing principle that precedes the law
views.case: Abram tithed before Moses, Genesis 14:20, and Jacob promised it, Genesis 28:22, so the practice is not merely Mosaic. Jesus did not set it aside, Matthew 23:23, and Hebrews 7 uses Abraham's tithe to argue for the greater priesthood of Melchizedek. On this view the tenth stays as a minimum, with freewill giving above it.

views.label: The standard is the spirit of the tithe, set higher by grace
views.case: A third view says the New Testament replaces the percentage with the example of Christ, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, and calls for proportionate and sacrificial giving. For some a tenth is a place to begin, for others far more, and the Jerusalem church shared possessions altogether, Acts 4:34 to 35.

debates.bearing: Whatever one concludes about the figure, the passage insists that God's people hold their possessions as His and give with trust, and that withholding what God has asked is a spiritual matter. The New Testament adds that giving is a response to grace and so is to be glad and generous, not grudging.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word beyond the basic text is huqqim, 'statutes,' in verse 7. The people have 'turned away' from them, a verb that means to turn aside from a path, and the call to 'return' is the opposite movement. The sin in view is not a single act but a long drift, 'from the days of your fathers.' What the prophet wants is a reversal of direction, and the tithe is where the reversal becomes visible.

The pairing in verse 8, 'tithes and offerings,' puts maaser, the tenth, next to terumah, the contribution or portion lifted off and set apart for God. The second word has the sense of something raised up as a gift, and it covers the share given to the priests from the produce. The theft is therefore of both the fixed tenth and the freewill portion, the required and the generous.

The word 'cursed' in verse 9 is a noun form, me'erah, and the phrase is an emphatic doubling, literally 'with the curse you are cursed.' It echoes the noun-and-verb construction of the covenant curses in Deuteronomy 28:15, and in 1:14 and 2:2 Malachi has used the related language of curse for the deceiver and the priests. The people are not under a new judgment but a standing one.

In verse 10 the 'storehouse' is otsar, a place where valuables or provisions are kept, and the same word appears for the temple's treasuries in the days of Nehemiah, Nehemiah 10:38. The reason for filling it is 'that there may be food in My house,' and the word for 'food' is teref, a word for provision to be eaten. The purpose is that the household of God, the Levites and priests, may eat. 'Windows of heaven' is arubbot, the same word used for the openings that released the flood, Genesis 7:11. The same image of the sky opening can mean destruction or blessing, and God gives it here as rain on a drought-stricken land.

The phrase translated 'blessing without measure' is literally, as the footnote notes, 'blessing for which there will be no room.' The sentence imagines a blessing too large for the barns. The 'devourer' in verse 11 is, as the BSB footnote says, probably a crop-destroying pest such as the locust, and the vine will not 'fail to produce fruit,' with a verb that describes miscarriage, as in Exodus 23:26 where no woman in the land would miscarry. The vine, in other words, will carry its fruit to term.

The final verse uses 'call you blessed,' a verb related to the Hebrew word of happiness found at the head of the Psalms, and 'a land of delight,' with the noun chefets, delight. The same noun was used of the Messenger 'in whom you delight' in 3:1, and in Isaiah 62:4 the land is given the name Hephzibah, a name that means my delight is in her, and is said to be the LORD's bride. God's delight in His land is the reason the nations will envy it.

typology.type: The storehouse and the food in God's house, Malachi 3:10
typology.fulfillment: The tithes were gathered so that God's servants could eat and live. In the church the principle is carried on, as Paul says the Lord commanded that 'those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel,' 1 Corinthians 9:14, and the collection for the saints in Jerusalem is described as sharing in spiritual and material things, Romans 15:26 to 27. The correspondence is care for those who serve God. The type falls short in that the Christian storehouse is not a building, and the house to be fed is a household of faith.

typology.type: The windows of heaven opened, Malachi 3:10
typology.fulfillment: The image of heaven opened to pour blessing on the people reaches fulfillment in the gift of the Holy Spirit poured out at Pentecost, Acts 2:17 and 33, and in the blessing that Paul says is already ours, 'every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms,' Ephesians 1:3. The escalation is from rain on a field to the Spirit in a heart. The type is partial, since material blessing is no longer promised as a result of obedience, and the fullness of what is promised awaits the age to come.

typology.type: The curse turned to blessing for the nations, Malachi 3:9 to 12
typology.fulfillment: The people lived under the curse of Deuteronomy 28 and the promise that all nations would call them blessed. Paul says that 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us' so that 'the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:13 to 14. The pattern of curse reversed and blessing reaching the nations is exactly this. The type is incomplete in Malachi because the land and its crops stand in for the blessing, and Christ gives the Spirit.

The demand to bring the whole tenth, at a price, is carried by the greater self-giving of Christ, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The widow who put in all she had, Mark 12:44, shows the same spirit in miniature. The correspondence is real but the direction is reversed: where Israel was asked to give to God, in Christ God gives to His people. It should not be pressed to make every gift a type of the cross.

study.christ:
The passage begins with the sentence on which everything else rests, 'I, the LORD, do not change.' The way that sentence leads to Christ is by pointing to the One who is the full expression of God's constancy. Hebrews 13:8 says 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever,' and Hebrews 6:17 to 18 speaks of God's purpose as unchangeable, guaranteed by an oath, so that 'we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged.' The God who did not destroy the descendants of Jacob, even though they deserved it, is the God whose faithfulness stands in Christ.

The passage also leads to Christ by the problem of the curse. The people are 'cursed with a curse,' and the story of the Old Testament is that they could not escape it by trying harder. Paul says Christ took it: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' so that the blessing promised to Abraham might come to the Gentiles, Galatians 3:13 to 14. Malachi's final promise, that all the nations will call Judah blessed, is the very thing the cross makes possible, since the blessing of Abraham reaches the nations through Christ. The robbery of verse 8 is also answered. The people took from God what was His, and Christ gave to God what was owed and what no one else could pay.

It leads to Christ by contrast in the matter of giving. God asked for a tenth and was robbed. God gave His Son and did not hold Him back. 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?' Romans 8:32. The one who calls for generosity is the One who set the pattern, and Paul builds his plea to the Corinthians on it: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The invitation to test God in verse 10 is answered once and for all in a gift beyond what any harvest could measure.

It leads to Christ by the 'food in My house.' Jesus is the bread from heaven, John 6:35, and the one who feeds those who serve Him. When He sends out the Twelve, He says 'the worker is worthy of his provisions,' Matthew 10:10. The abundance that Malachi pictured in barns and vats is a shadow of the fullness found in Him.

Guarding against overreach matters especially here. The passage is not a hidden prediction of the cross in every detail, and it is not a promise that Christ will make His followers rich. Jesus Himself taught that a person's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions, Luke 12:15, and told the rich young man to give to the poor, Mark 10:21. The link to Christ is by the character of the unchanging God, the reversal of the curse, and the pattern of generous self-giving, which the text itself raises.
study.god:
Everything here depends on the sentence at the start: 'I, the LORD, do not change.' It does not say that God is unmoved, since the next verses show Him calling, pleading, accusing and promising. It says that His character and purpose do not shift with the people's behaviour. Numbers 23:19 states the same truth, that God is not 'a son of man, that He should change His mind.' This constancy is what keeps the descendants of Jacob from being consumed, as Lamentations 3:22 puts it, because of the LORD's loving devotion. Without it there would be no hope for a people who had failed for generations.

He is a God who invites return and returns. 'Return to Me, and I will return to you.' The same offer is made in Zechariah 1:3. God is not waiting with arms folded. He moves toward those who move toward Him, and in the story of the prodigal son the father runs while the son is still a long way off, Luke 15:20. God's constancy is therefore not stillness but faithfulness in the same direction.

He is an owner. The accusation 'You are robbing Me' assumes that the tithe belongs to God, and the whole of Scripture grounds that claim. 'The earth is the LORD's, and the fullness thereof,' Psalm 24:1. David said as much when the people gave for the temple: 'everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You,' 1 Chronicles 29:14. God asks for a tenth not because He is short of anything but because the act of giving declares who owns the harvest. It is a recognition that all of it is His.

He is honest about the cost of sin. The curse of verse 9 is the plain outcome of a broken relationship, and God does not hide it. Yet He is also honest about His heart, because the tone of the passage is not of a man who loves money but a Father who wants to bless. The final verses are all promise, a land of delight and a people the nations call blessed.

He is generous without measure. The phrase 'blessing without measure' in verse 10 and the image of heaven's windows open describe a giver whose supply exceeds any capacity to hold it. And He is patient to be tested. A God who says 'Test Me' is not fragile. He is confident enough in His own goodness to put it on trial in the ordinary matter of what a farmer does with his grain.

In worship this means that giving is among the plainest acts of worship, an acknowledgement that He is our provider. It also means that anxiety about provision is a form of distrust that God addresses by pointing to His own character. We give not to earn but because the One who asks does not change and has already given everything.

crossReferences.note: The same reciprocal offer, 'Return to Me, declares the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you,' given at the start of the rebuilding period. Read beside Malachi 3:7 it shows that the call to return was the core message of the whole post-exilic prophetic ministry and that God's promise to come back was as constant as His call.

Jacob's vow at Bethel, that of all God gives him he will give a tenth. God calls the people 'descendants of Jacob' in Malachi 3:6, and there is a quiet reproach in it: they have failed to keep the vow their ancestor made when he had nothing but a stone for a pillow.

The Levites receive all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance for their service, and they in turn give a tithe of the tithe to the priests. It explains who was harmed when the tithes were withheld in Malachi's day, and why the prophet speaks of food in God's house.

The curse on the disobedient includes seed sown but little harvested, locusts that consume the crop and vines whose grapes are eaten by worms. It is the background for the 'devourer' of Malachi 3:11, and shows that the loss the people feared was the loss their withholding brought.

Nehemiah finds that the Levites' portions have not been given and they have gone back to their fields, and he asks, 'Why has the house of God been neglected?' It is a historical window onto the same neglect, and the result after he acts, all Judah bringing a tenth into the storerooms, is the fulfilment of the command of Malachi 3:10.

God tells the people to consider how things went before they rebuilt the temple, when twenty measures became ten, and promises 'from this day on, I will bless you.' It is the clearest earlier parallel to Malachi 3:10 to 12, and shows that putting God's house first is bound up with the reversal of poor harvests.

'Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your harvest.' The wisdom tradition states the promise of Malachi as a principle of life, with barns filled and vats overflowing, and reminds us that Proverbs speaks of general patterns, not guarantees.

Jesus tells the scribes and Pharisees they should have practiced justice, mercy and faithfulness 'without neglecting' the tithe. It shows that He did not abolish the practice but set it within the heart of the law, and it warns against making giving a substitute for compassion.

Paul says whoever sows generously reaps generously, that each should give 'not out of regret or compulsion,' and that God loves a cheerful giver. It is the New Testament form of Malachi's teaching, with the percentage gone and the heart foregrounded, and a promise that God supplies what is needed for every good work.

The churches of Macedonia gave beyond their ability out of deep poverty, having first given themselves to the Lord. They are the proof that the principle of Malachi 3 is trust and not return on investment, since their giving was joyful and came from poverty.

Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles. It is the New Testament account of how the curse of Malachi 3:9 gives way to the blessing of 3:12, and how the nations come to be blessed.

study.oneStory:
The first thing the story of the Bible says about God and wealth is that all of it was given. Eden is a garden of provision, with every tree for food and one set apart, Genesis 2:16 to 17. The first sin is, in one of its aspects, a refusal to leave the one thing that belonged to God as His. Malachi's charge of robbery is therefore an old story retold: a people with everything again reaching for the share that was never theirs.

The tithe appears as the answer, a way of saying with a tenth of the harvest that the whole is a gift. Abram does it before the law, Genesis 14:20, and Jacob vows it with only a stone to rest on, Genesis 28:22. The law gathers it into the life of a nation that is to be a kingdom of priests, with the Levites supported so that they may serve and the vulnerable fed in the third year. Israel's calling was to show the nations what it looks like to live under a generous God, and verse 12 says that is exactly what the nations would see: 'all the nations will call you blessed.' That echoes the promise to Abraham, 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3.

The story of Israel, however, is the story of a nation that did not do this. Malachi speaks near the end of the Old Testament, to a people who have come back from exile and still will not trust. What the passage sets up is the need for a different kind of giving, from a different kind of heart. 'I, the LORD, do not change' means that the promise to Abraham is not cancelled by the people's failure, and the blessing has to arrive by another route.

Christ is that route. He becomes a curse so that the blessing reaches the nations, Galatians 3:13 to 14. The poverty He took on makes His people rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The Spirit poured out at Pentecost fulfils the heavens opened, Acts 2:33, and the church that gives itself first to the Lord, 2 Corinthians 8:5, becomes the community in which generosity is the mark of a people who know they have been given everything.

The story ends in a world with no more curse, where the nations bring their glory into the city and the tree of life bears fruit every month, Revelation 22:2 to 3. The scarcity that made tithing a test is gone, and the God who does not change is present with His people. What began in a garden of gift ends in a city of gift, and what the nations saw dimly in Judah's blessing they see fully, in the unveiled goodness of the One who has never changed.

sermon.title: Malachi's Message On Stewardship (Malachi's Modern Message Part 6)
sermon.why: The sixth message of Legge's expository series through Malachi, covering 3:7-12, the heart of this disputation. It handles the call to return, the charge of robbing God, and the invitation to test Him, guarding against a prosperity reading and pointing to the generous, unchanging God revealed in Christ.

quiz.q: On what truth does God ground His appeal in this passage?

options.text: That He does not change, which is why His faithless people have not been destroyed.
options.note: Verse 6 makes God's unchanging character the basis of His mercy and His call.

options.text: That the people had earned a second chance.
options.note: Their survival rests on God's constancy, not their merit.

options.text: That the temple was now complete.
options.note: The ground is God's unchanging nature, not the finished building.

options.text: That the harvest had already improved.
options.note: The blessing is promised as they obey; the ground is God's changelessness.

quiz.q: How were the people robbing God?

options.text: By withholding the tithes and offerings that belonged to Him.
options.note: Verse 8 names tithes and offerings as the theft from God.

options.text: By stealing from the temple treasury directly.
options.note: The robbery was withholding what was owed, not breaking into the treasury.

options.text: By refusing to offer any sacrifices at all.
options.note: The charge is specifically about withheld tithes and offerings.

options.text: By overpaying the priests.
options.note: The opposite: they were keeping back what God required.

quiz.q: What is striking about God's words test Me in this?

options.text: God, who rarely invites testing, calls His people to prove His faithfulness by obedient giving.
options.note: Verse 10 offers a rare invitation to test God's generosity through obedience.

options.text: God is offering a formula guaranteeing personal wealth.
options.note: It calls for trust and obedience, not a transaction for riches.

options.text: God is daring them to sin and see what happens.
options.note: He invites obedience, not sin; the test is wholehearted giving.

options.text: God forbids ever trusting Him for provision.
options.note: The verse does the opposite, inviting them to trust His provision.

quiz.q: How should this passage be applied today?

options.text: As a call to trust God's provision and give generously, not as a formula for guaranteed wealth.
options.note: The New Testament reframes giving as cheerful and generous, trusting the faithful Provider.

options.text: As a promise that every gift returns a financial profit.
options.note: That prosperity reading misuses the text; the heart is trust, not gain.

options.text: As a rule that Christians must tithe exactly ten percent or be cursed.
options.note: The tithe law was given to Israel; the New Testament calls for proportionate, cheerful giving.

options.text: As irrelevant, since God no longer cares about our giving.
options.note: God still calls His people to trust Him with their resources.

quiz.q: How is the unchanging God of verse 6 revealed in Christ?

options.text: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, the steadfast mercy that spares sinners.
options.note: Hebrews 13:8 identifies Christ with the unchanging God of this verse.

options.text: Christ shows that God changes His mind constantly.
options.note: The opposite: Christ reveals God's unchanging faithfulness.

options.text: Christ makes God's promises uncertain.
options.note: In Christ every promise is Yes; His constancy secures them.

options.text: Christ has no link to God's changelessness.
options.note: He is the very expression of the unchanging God.

questions: God says because I do not change, you have not been destroyed. How does God's unchanging faithfulness give you security when your own faithfulness wavers?
God calls, return to Me and I will return to you. Is there an area where you have drifted and need to turn back, trusting that God moves toward those who move toward Him?
The people withheld from God what was His. What does your giving reveal about whether you trust God as your provider or lean on your possessions?
God invited His people to test His faithfulness through obedience. Where is God calling you to step out in trust and prove His provision rather than playing it safe?
We cannot out-give the God who gave His own Son. How does the generosity of God in Christ free you to hold your resources with open hands?

translationNotes.note: I the LORD do not change affirms God's constancy of character and covenant, the ground of His mercy toward the descendants of Jacob.
Blessing without measure carries a BSB footnote noting the literal sense, blessing for which there will be no room, a picture of overflowing abundance.
The devourer carries a BSB footnote noting it is probably a name for a crop-destroying pest, such as locusts, that God promises to rebuke.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Malachi 3:6-12. All 7 verses reproduced in order. BSB footnotes at 3:10 (literal blessing for which there will be no room) and 3:11 (the devourer as a crop-destroying pest) are reflected in the translation notes.
